conversation.content:
Hello—thank you for making time to talk today. I’m Dr. Bennett, a perinatal-mental-health clinician. My job is simply to listen and to help you feel supported as you settle into new motherhood.

To guide our conversation, I’ll be using a brief screening tool called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**, or EPDS for short. It’s a set of 10 questions designed to capture how you’ve been feeling over the past seven days. There are no right or wrong answers; we just want to understand your experience so we can offer the best care possible.

Everything you share is confidential and stays between you and the care team—except in the very rare instance we feel you might be in immediate danger, in which case we would work together on next steps to keep you safe.

We’ll keep this relaxed and conversational. I’ll re-phrase each question in everyday language, and you can answer however feels most comfortable. Ready to begin?

**Question 1:**  
Over the past week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

*settles back in the chair, giving a small shrug*

I guess... I've laughed a little? My husband made a joke about the baby's diaper explosions the other night and I did chuckle. But mostly it feels like I'm just going through the motions. Things that used to seem hilarious before the baby was born just don't hit the same anymore. It's like I can recognize when something is supposed to be funny, but I don't really feel it in my chest like I used to.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

*gives a small nod*

Yeah… I can still laugh sometimes—like when my husband joked about the diaper “blow-outs.” But mostly it feels forced or far away, not that warm, easy feeling I used to get.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

*shifts a bit, eyes dropping to my lap*

Not really… I mean, I *want* to look forward to stuff—like taking the baby for walks or meeting a friend for coffee—but when the time comes, it just feels flat. I’ll think, “This should be nice,” yet I’m mostly tired or worrying about whether the baby will fuss. Even little things I used to get excited about—like my favorite show or a shower without interruptions—don’t spark much anymore.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

*sighs softly*

Sometimes... like last night when the baby wouldn't settle for hours. I kept thinking maybe it's because I ate something that upset his stomach, or I'm not holding him right. When he finally fell asleep, instead of feeling relieved, I just kept replaying everything in my head, wondering what I did wrong. I know logically that babies just cry sometimes, but there's still this little voice saying I should have figured it out faster.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

*wrings my hands in my lap*

Yeah... most days. Like, I'll be feeding the baby and suddenly my heart starts racing because I'm sure something's wrong—even when he's perfectly fine. Last night I couldn't sleep because I kept checking if he was breathing. I know it's normal to worry, but these feelings come out of nowhere and feel so strong. Sometimes I get this tightness in my chest that won't go away, even when everything seems okay.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

*presses a hand to my chest*

Sometimes—especially at night. I’ll be rocking the baby and suddenly feel like I can’t catch my breath, like something awful is about to happen even though everything’s quiet. My heart starts pounding and I get this rush of “what-if” thoughts—what if he stops breathing, what if I drop him, what if I’m just not cut out for this. It passes after a few minutes, but in the moment it feels so real and scary.
Things have been getting on top of me

*nods slowly, exhaling*

Yeah… most days feel like I’m barely treading water. I’ll finally get the baby down, then notice the sink’s full of bottles, the laundry’s overflowing, and I haven’t eaten anything but a granola bar. I’ll think, “I should be able to handle this,” but it piles up so fast. Sometimes I just sit there staring at the mess, too tired to move, telling myself I’ll do it in five minutes… and an hour later nothing’s done and I feel worse.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

*hesitates, eyes flicking to the window*

I wouldn’t call it “unhappy,” exactly… more like my mind won’t shut off. I’ll lie down after the baby’s finally asleep, but then I start replaying every little thing—did I fasten the swaddle right, did I sanitize the pump parts, am I doing any of this right?—and suddenly it’s two a.m. and I’m still wide awake. Even when I do drift off, I wake up at every tiny grunt or squeak over the monitor. So I’m exhausted, but wired at the same time.
I have felt sad or miserable

*shrugs one shoulder, voice quiet*

I guess… yeah, some days. It’s not there every minute, but it kind of hits out of nowhere—like I’ll be folding onesies and just feel this heaviness settle in. I start thinking I should be happier, everyone says these weeks are so special, and that just makes me feel worse. I end up tearing up for a bit, then I wipe my face and keep going. It’s not all day, but it keeps popping back in.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

*bites lip, looks down*

Not really… I mean, I’ve teared up a couple of times, like when I couldn’t get him to latch or when my mom left after visiting, but actual crying? Maybe once this week. Mostly I just feel that thick, achy sadness stuck in my throat without it spilling over. I keep thinking if I start I might not stop, so I blink hard and swallow it down.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

*shakes head quickly*

No—never. I’ve felt overwhelmed and tired, sure, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself. My baby needs me, and even on the hardest days that’s the one thing that feels clear.

You've shared how the early weeks with your baby have felt heavy and overwhelming: laughter feels distant, excitement has faded, and most days bring a swirl of worry and self-doubt. Even simple tasks-folding laundry, making a meal-can feel insurmountable, especially when your mind races at night and sadness keeps creeping in. You love your baby deeply and are doing your very best, yet you're also running on empty and wondering whether these feelings are part of "normal" new-mother exhaustion.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 21, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Laughing feels forced or distant, clearly less than before, matching "Definitely not so much now"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes almost complete loss of anticipatory joy and emotional flatness, matching "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>"Yes, some of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes daily, intense, physiologic anxiety that arises without trigger, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden nighttime episodes of breathlessness, racing heart, and catastrophic "what-if" thoughts that resolve in minutes, matching "Yes, sometimes."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes feeling overwhelmed "most days," unable to manage basic tasks, and stuck in a cycle of inaction and worsening mood, aligning with "most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes near-nightly intrusive worries keeping her awake until 2 a.m. and repeated waking, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes recurrent waves of sadness that interrupt daily tasks, occur "quite often," and trigger tearfulness—matching "Yes, quite often."</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 21 on the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale meets the cut-off for probable major depression. You described core symptoms consistent with <med>Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>: diminished interest or pleasure (<sym>laughter feels forced/far away</sym>, anticipatory enjoyment "flat" nearly every day), prominent self-blame, psychomotor slowing, fatigue, recurrent sadness, and difficulty sleeping unrelated to infant care. Additionally, you experience near-daily <sym>anxiety</sym> and nocturnal <sym>panic episodes</sym> that resolve quickly but cause significant distress. While you have no self-harm ideation, functional impairment is evident (<quote>I'm barely treading water</quote>). This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Schedule an urgent appointment with your <med>primary care provider</med> or an obstetric clinician this week; bring a copy of your EPDS results
2. Ask about evidence-based treatments such as <med>CBT</med>, brief interpersonal therapy, or sertraline (compatible with breastfeeding)
3. Contact Postpartum Support International 24/7 warm-line (1-800-944-4773) or text "HELP" to 800-944-4773 for local resources and peer support
4. Arrange practical help-partner, friend, or doula-to cover one night feeding so you can obtain a 4-5-hour stretch of sleep
5. Practice 5-minute grounding exercises (slow diaphragmatic breathing, naming five things you can see) when <sym>panic sensations</sym> arise
6. Keep brief daily mood/anxiety logs to track patterns for your next visit
7. Screen again in two weeks or sooner if symptoms worsen
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 21: Screening Note – Postpartum Episode (not diagnostic)

Patient-reported symptoms (2–3 wks post-delivery):

<sym>Depressive features</sym>
– Marked anhedonia: minimal enjoyment in previously pleasurable activities; laughter feels “forced/far away.”
– Episodic sad/miserable mood with tearfulness; guilt/self-blame re infant care (“should have figured it out faster”).
– Sleep disruption driven by ruminating and hypervigilance, not solely infant demands.

<sym>Anxiety features</sym>
– Near-daily, unprovoked anxious arousal: racing heart, breathlessness, catastrophic “what-if” cognitions.
– Nocturnal panic spells while infant is calm; rapid resolution but high distress.

<sym>Functioning</sym>
– Feels “barely treading water”; household tasks accumulate, contributing to sense of failure.
– No self-harm ideation; protective factor = strong infant attachment.

Pattern: symptoms present most days, cause subjective impairment, exceed “typical” postpartum adjustment.

Screening significance: meets threshold for probable <med>postpartum depression</med> with prominent <med>anxiety</med>; low safety risk at present. Recommend formal assessment (PHQ-9/EPDS, clinical interview) and psychoeducation/support planning.
